Our tourism sector has a friendliness problem. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On paper, the launch of a three-month tourism carnival in Cox's Bazar is a welcome initiative.
Featuring cultural performances, adventure activities, food festivals, beach sports, and family entertainment, the event reflects a recognition that tourism must be about experiences rather than merely destinations.
With that said, Bangladesh's tourism challenge has never been a lack of attractions.
From the world's longest natural sea beach to the Sundarbans, tea gardens, archaeological sites, hill tracts, rivers, and rich cultural heritage, Bangladesh has always possessed tourism assets. The problem is that possessing attractions and being a tourist-friendly destination are not the same thing.
What we have failed to recognize is the importance of the visitor experience itself. Tourists, whether domestic or international, need more than events and slogans. They need safety, cleanliness, reliable transportation, clear information, quality accommodation, and confidence that they can enjoy their trip without harassment, fraud, or unnecessary inconvenience.
Sadly, we have never quite been able to provide that.
This is especially important for women travellers and families. A destination cannot truly thrive if visitors constantly have to worry about personal security, overcrowding, poor waste management, or inadequate emergency services.
Tourism flourishes where people feel comfortable, welcomed, and protected. These should not be viewed as ancillary issues but rather as the foundation of any serious tourism strategy.
Bangladesh must move beyond treating tourism as a seasonal activity or a series of promotional events. It should be developed as a major economic sector capable of creating jobs, attracting investment, and improving the country's international image.
However, that will require sustained investment in infrastructure, training for service providers, environmental protection, law enforcement, and visitor-friendly governance.
Bangladesh’s tourism sector has long had the potential. But that will only be possible when we can provide a safe, clean, and welcoming environment.

item.title: The need to confront violence against women. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh has spent decades celebrating gains in girls' education, women's employment, and political representation. Yet behind these achievements lies a grim reality we all-too-often ignore: Violence against women remains one of the country's most pervasive and persistent injustices.
Progress cannot be measured solely by economic indicators when millions of women continue to face violence in their homes, workplaces, educational institutions, and online spaces.
This year's theme,"Speak out. Believe survivors. Demand justice," arrives at a moment when silence remains one of the greatest enablers of abuse.
Too often in our nation, public discussions focus on a survivor's conduct rather than a perpetrator's crime.
Too often, women are advised to be more careful instead of men being told to stop abusing.
Victim-blaming remains deeply embedded in our social fabric, discouraging reporting and shielding perpetrators from accountability. If we are to be taken seriously as a nation that is making progress, such regressive attitudes will simply not do.
The problem extends beyond social attitudes. Impunity remains a stubborn reality. Despite the countless documented cases of rape and domestic violence, that we continue to see such an alarming gap between legal protections and their enforcement is telling of how much work needs to be done on this front.
Bangladesh does not lack laws. What it lacks is consistent implementation, survivor-centred support services, timely investigations, and swift justice. Shelters, legal aid, counselling, and protection mechanisms remain inadequate for many women, especially those who need them most.
A nation with aspirations such as ours cannot tolerate a culture where violence against half its population is normalized and who are consistently questioned and doubted. Speaking out against misogyny, believing those who come forward, and demanding accountability from institutions is the bare minimum we can do.

item.title: Rohail Nazir's fifty books Asia Cup Rising Stars semi-finals spot for Pakistan Shaheens. [ dawn ]
item.description:
An unbeaten half-century by Rohail Nazir, followed by a devastating bowling display, helped Pakistan Shaheens defeat Nepal by 96 runs in their final Group ‘B’ match of the Asia Cup Rising Stars at the University of Doha for Science and Technology on Tuesday.

The defending champions remained unbeaten in the tournament, winning all three of their group matches to qualify for the semi-finals, where they will face Bangladesh A on Nov 27.

Batting first, Pakistan Shaheens were in trouble at 66-6 in 16.5 overs before wicket-keeper-batter Rohail steadied the innings with an unbeaten 64 off 83 balls, hitting four fours and three sixes.

After Hasan Nawaz fell for 28 off 59 balls, leaving the Shaheens at 88-7, Rohail added 70 runs for the eighth wicket with Ahmed Daniyal, who scored 16 off 35 balls, to help his side reach 168 before being bowled out in 42 overs.

For Nepal, Rashid Khan claimed five wickets for 39 runs, while Abhishesh Gautam took two.

Nepal’s chase got off to a disastrous start as Muhammad Imran and Mohammad Hasnain reduced them to 15-4 inside six overs. Hasnain struck twice in successive deliveries to dismiss Ishan Pandey and Lokesh Bam without scoring.

Left-arm spinner Sufyan Moqim then claimed three wickets as Nepal slumped to 59-9. Mayan Yadav offered some resistance with a top score of 41 off 50 balls but was trapped leg-before by Maaz Sadaqat as Nepal were dismissed for 72 in 17.3 overs.

Hasnain and Sufyan took three wickets each for 21 and 17 runs respectively, while Imran claimed two for 29.

Rohail was named player of the match for his match-winning innings.

item.title: Liberté, égalité, fatigué—the young are tired of everyone. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The writing was on the wall. Calls for mobilisation on 17 October had been followed by viral videos, parodying Japanese anime and Marvel productions to rally the troops. The streets had caught on: with each new day of mobilisation, walls became covered in angry, audacious graffiti, ranging from ‘F@ck the 17 (the generic number for the French police), bring on the 17th’ to ‘17 October, better than October 17 (the second of two revolutions in Russia in 1917)’.

When the day finally arrived, a perfect storm swept across France, from its largest metropolitan areas to its mid-sized towns. High school and university students, who had been mobilising for weeks, took to the streets in large numbers. They were joined by demonstrators protesting the rising cost of living, including some associating themselves with the Yellow Vest movement, as well as by French and foreign far-left activists. All in all, between 550,000 and 800,000 persons went into the streets on that day. In the violence that ensued, some turned on police forces and official buildings, while others targeted small businesses and department stores. Mass looting and damage to public buildings, including the town halls of Limoges and Marseille, led the government to impose curfews in several cities over the next few days.

In each city, even in each neighbourhood, this day of mobilisation took on a different character, depending on the composition of the crowds and their interactions with the police. In some parts of Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Nantes, Rennes or Bordeaux, the attacks against police forces and government buildings took a quasi-insurrectional character. Elsewhere, the riots were more reminiscent of the ordered disorder of carnival. As law enforcement remained at a distance, the streets were left to jubilant protesters, often dressed up in costumes. In this space wrested from the ordinary constraints of everyday life, the Republican motto of ‘liberté, égalité, fraternité’ (liberty, equality, fraternity) suddenly took a new meaning as protesters of different ages, classes and racial backgrounds revelled in the furious spectacle of their momentary unity. This subversion of the protest order — it was no longer the demonstration that overflowed, but the overflow that demonstrated — nevertheless remained contained within certain bounds. In the parts of Paris that I walked through, at least, vehicles and shops were not set on fire and the forces of disorder remained somewhat contained, at least until the looting began.

This day of wrath and jubilation will probably not be repeated soon. The stars that aligned on that day have since then changed their orbit. Suburban youths, many of them first-time protesters, have not been durably integrated into street protests, while the intensity of repression deterred more privileged youths from repeating the experience of the 17th. In the following weeks, the mobilisation thus took a less belligerent turn and returned to a more conventional social movement led by student and labour unions. In many lycées, however, blockades persist and tensions are rising between mobilised students and parents worrying about the impact of a prolonged closure of the schools.

A clap of thunder in a troubled sky

Calls for a mobilisation against ‘la vie chère’ (high cost of living) started circulating on social media in September 2026, autonomously from the labour unions that traditionally organise demonstrations in France. In September 2025, a similar attempt to ‘block everything’ across the country was a failure and French intelligence agencies did not take the hype around 17 October seriously. They miscalculated the amplifying effect of the student movement, without which this call to action would probably have fizzled out.

In September 2026, a nationwide movement of high school and university students started calling for better teaching conditions, including increased teaching staff and renovated school buildings. The mobilisation was also fuelled by a deep crisis within the French higher education system. In 1980, only 40 per cent of a whole age group obtained the baccalaureate. Today, 80 per cent obtain this prestigious school-leaving certificate, leading to severe pressure on higher education institutions. Rather than the increase of baccalaureate-holders per se, stagnant state funding of universities and limited vocational education options have severely constrained the access to higher education. While asking for 200,000 new positions in universities, high school students have also been asking for the suppression of Parcoursup, the pre-enrolment platform for first-year higher education programmes, which they see as opaque, discriminatory and stressful.

By protesting underfunding of high schools and universities, mobilised students also defended an idea of public education as a public good. As Leila, a 12th grade student in the 9th arrondissement of Paris, told me while sitting on a dustbin during the blockade of her high school on 5 November, “We are calling for pay rises for our supervisors, our cleaners and our teachers. We cannot expect teachers to work themselves to the bone if their salaries do not reflect the effort they put in. Our teachers are the backbone of education and teaching. And education is a weapon against disinformation and the dumbing down of society.”

The movement initially started in late August in Mayotte, an overseas department and region located in the Indian Ocean, before expanding to impoverished suburbs of the Greater Paris region, such as Créteil and Saint-Denis. With a significant number of them of North African or Sub-Saharan African descent, local students denounced the unkept promises of the French meritocratic system of education. By draping themselves in the national flag or singing the national anthem in protests, they reiterated their attachment to egalitarian ideals, while pointing out the systemic discrimination undermining the professed ideal of equal opportunity for descendants of postcolonial immigrants. By early October, the protests expanded to more privileged sections of the youths, including the so-called ‘jeunesse dorée’ (golden youth) attending the most prestigious public schools. Expressing solidarity with suburban youths, students from city centres shared their concern with the clogging of higher education, their anxieties towards the possibilities of the far-right Rassemblement National coming to power in 2027, as well as more diffuse fears towards a future compromised by the compounding threats of climate change, armed conflict and artificial intelligence.

Even if it does not yet translate into joint structures of mobilisation transcending deep social, racial and residential divides, the sense of unity among this anxious youth is palpable. Besides shared concerns specific to this age group, it is rooted in demographic transformations. In 2026, the number of people aged 65 and over became nearly equal to the number of those under 20, and this trend toward a demographic reversal will only intensify in the next decades. By 2070, 32 per cent of the population will be 65 or older — twice the proportion of those under 20. In this ageing society, which it holds responsible for the current state of world affairs, the youth feel belittled and silenced.

The brutal repression of the movement only added fuel to the fire. During the first weeks of October, protests spread to numerous high schools and universities, many of which were subsequently blockaded across the country. In the meantime, increasing price of petrol at the pumps and rising costs of living more generally stoked concerns about purchasing power. This led young influencers and activists to call for a resumption of the Yellow Vest movement, which was prompted by similar concerns in 2018. As 17 October approached, clashes with the police multiplied around high schools and during street demonstrations. In many cities, the atmosphere was electric.

Joyful anger

In its early phase and even more so on 17 October, this social movement disrupted the rules of political contention in France. Like the Yellow Vests before them, students initially evaded the control of labour unions that, historically, have been leading protests, articulating claims and negotiating with governmental authorities. Instead, high school and university students were mobilised by content on social media and they organised horizontally, through messaging applications like Snapchat. Their privileged forms of action were blockades and, to a lesser extent, wildcat demonstrations. Every morning, students would collect dustbins and building materials to block the entrance of their school, sometimes before going on an unauthorised demonstration across the area. On 1 October, I attended one such event in Saint-Denis, in the northern periphery of Paris. After assembling near Lycée Paul Éluard, about 200 high school and university students walked — and occasionally ran — across the town, visiting one high school after the other to mobilise other students. The mood was joyful but resolute: while provoking the police chasing them, students laughed, sang and delivered fiery speeches. Among the protesting students was a young boy dressed as Spider-Man and wearing a motorcycle helmet. Sitting on a dustbin pushed by jubilant teenagers, he was the focus of attention and added a dash of colour among young men and women often dressed in black and wearing surgical masks to protect themselves against tear gas.

As the movement expanded, student and labour unions started joining the fray and organising massive demonstrations across the country. These protests were more conventional in nature, and easier to manage for law enforcement. The large participation of high school and university students, however, endowed them with an energy and a creativity evading the usual mobilisations of labour unions. Expanding on a protest repertoire that emerged during the movement against the reform of pension laws in 2023, young participants brought placards with ironic, witty slogans drawing from various sources of influence: the Revolution of 1789, the protest movement of May 1968, as well as social media and popular culture. The reclaiming of revolutionary symbols — the caps of the sans-culottes, the guillotine, Liberty leading the people — coexisted with references to video games such as Mario Bros, Legend of Zelda or GTA, to popular film series such as Star Wars and the Hunger Games, as well as to more contemporary Internet memes and ‘brain rot’. Some of the slogans were franchised: after circulating on social media, they were picked up by young protesters, who in the process reaffirmed their belonging to a protest community united by shared cultural references.

As Céline, a student at EPSA, the Paris school of graphic design and visual communication, explained during a demonstration on 5 November, “popular culture allows you to convey political messages more easily, because everyone has the reference”. On that day, she was herself dressed up as Luigi, the secondary protagonist of the video game franchise Mario Bros, and she carried a placard showing this popular character removing President Emmanuel Macron and the far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen with a vacuum cleaner.

Indeed, beyond making claims for better working conditions in lycées and universities, these youthful protests have also been directed against the far right and the imminent threat of its access to power after the presidential elections of May 2027. Besides a general sense of dread towards an uncertain future, this threat has been a major unifier among the youth, across social and racial divides. Drawn from a song by the 1980s punk band Bérurier Noir, ‘La jeunesse emmerde le Front National’ (The youth tells the Front National [the original name of the Rassemblement National] to f@ck off) remains one of the popular anthems among the protesters, although a new one emerged in early November, ‘J’ai deux passions, la fanfare, la révolution’ (I have two passions: the brass band and the revolution!).

‘Everyone hates the police’, but the police have many friends

Both joyful and belligerent, this social movement has met with unprecedented levels of repression, which has fuelled hostility, even hatred towards the police. As of 17 November, at least 155 protesters or passers-by had suffered serious injuries by the explosive weapons used by law enforcement — including 11 eye losses, seven amputations and 18 fractured skulls. The number of arrests has also reached unprecedented levels: between mid-September and mid-November 2026, more than 12,000 protesters were sent to custody, most of them minors. By comparison, 6,730 protesters met the same fate during the 2018–2019 movement of the Yellow Vests, 890 during the protests against the reform of labour laws in 2016, 150 during the student movement against the Loi Devaquet in 1986 and only 95 during the uprising of May 1968.

Far from restraining law enforcement officers, the Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has encouraged them to show “no restraint” when dealing with the protesters, whatever their age. Meanwhile, the Minister for Justice, Gérald Darmanin, has asked judges to be “merciless” with looters and rioters, especially after the events of 17 October. By and large, the judges have obliged and the judicial repression of the movement has been extremely severe, with large numbers of protesters being sent to jail for petty offences. During the days that followed 17 October, drastic measures were also taken to contain the protests.

Incidents of police violence have been widely publicised among the youths, through social media in particular. This has fuelled detestation of the police, exemplified by popular slogans heard at every demonstration: ‘ACAB’ (All Cops Are Bastards) or ‘Tout le monde déteste la police’ (Everyone hates the police).

Everyone does not hate the police in France, though. As a recent opinion poll by the Centre for Political Research at Sciences Po (CEVIPOF) shows, the level of confidence in the police remains high, at 73 per cent. Moreover, as violence escalated during protests and blockades dragged on, a growing number of individuals started volunteering to lend a strong hand to the police. Following the mass lootings that took place on 17 and 18 October, some influencers launched platforms to gather volunteers in support of shopkeepers. While the individuals behind these initiatives claimed to be politically neutral and to act in accordance with the law, the reality on the ground was rather different. On 24 October, as new protests were organised across the country, far-right militants assaulted demonstrators in a dozen cities under the pretext of protecting shopkeepers. Not only did the police refrain from interfering, in several cities, they actively collaborated with far-right groups, who delivered protesters to the men in blue after roughing them up. In Montpellier, a couple of days later, a judge sentenced one of these protesters to a suspended prison term after acknowledging that he had been arrested “by a militia“. After these collusions were exposed, several investigations were launched and far-right extremists became less visible in the following weeks, but the threat lingers on.

As high school blockades dragged on in many large cities, some parents also started acting as auxiliaries of law enforcement, if not as vigilantes taking the law in their own hands. Especially after the government of Sébastien Lecornu granted a few concessions to protesting students on 28 October — including a reform of Parcoursup and the creation of 15,000 additional seats in higher education — some parents started claiming that their children had been taken hostage by a minority of unyielding extremists. Some of these parents were also concerned about the challenge to authority — that of the state, as well as their own — posed by the student revolt. In Paris, Bordeaux, Marseille, Rennes or Montpellier, these infuriated parents organised on WhatsApp groups and started waking up at dawn to help the police contain the blockers. Forming human chains to protect students willing to go to class, they also tussled over the control of dustbins used by protesting students to block their lycées. In the ensuing scuffle, some students were hit and verbally abused by parents.

At Lycée Carnot, a prestigious public school in the 17th arrondissement of Paris, students told me that one of their schoolmates was the target of racist insults, while another received intimidating messages on his phone. For Adrien, a Senior Year student at Carnot, “These parents try to take the law into their own hands and, by doing so, they escalate violence because they make everyone furious.” School authorities are aware of this threat and the principal of another lycée in the 8th arrondissement, who asked to remain anonymous, said that he feared the opening of a “third front”, after those of students and cops, due to the counter-mobilisation of these parents.

Besides the risks of violent escalation, these initiatives seem to have mixed results. However menacing they try to be, parents are often outsmarted by the kids, who may give up blocking their school from outside only to foment trouble from within, leading school authorities to suspend activities anyway. As a result, hundreds of high schools (out of a total of 3,700) continue to be disturbed in the country — a figure which is difficult to verify since the Ministry of Education systematically scales down its statistics to convince public opinion that order has been restored. Whatever the exact figure, the return to normalcy remains elusive in many public schools and universities. While the kind of violence and looting witnessed on 17 October has not returned, tens of thousands of protesters continue to take to the streets every Saturday in major cities, with occasional skirmishes between them and the riot police.

Another Gen Z protest?

This ongoing student mobilisation shares characteristics with recent movements led by the Gen Z (composed of those born between 1997 and 2012) in Indonesia, Bangladesh, Nepal, Madagascar, Morocco or Peru. In France, even if labour unions started co-organising the protests from October 2026 onwards, the mobilisation has primarily involved youths between the ages of 15 and 25 years. This has infused it with a youthful energy and an irreverence characteristic of similar protests in the Global South and, more recently, across Europe (in Albania, Belgium, Italy and Germany). Especially in its early phase, the movement shared its horizontality with other youth revolts organised through Internet forums and communication apps such as LIHKG during the 2019 anti-ELAB movement in Hong Kong or Discord during more recent protests in Nepal and Morocco.

French students also draw on global cultural references that have provided young protesters worldwide with powerful role models. As Issa, a twenty-something protester who likes to dress up as Luffy, the main protagonist of One Piece, explained to me, “Luffy is the character who embodies freedom the best. He is devoted to living a free life. At the same time, he always cares for others. Whether in the manga or the anime, he always puts the interests of others ahead of his own, and those of the have nots ahead of those of the haves.” Coming from a Japanese manga and popularised by young Indonesians as a symbol of youthful rebellion, Luffy and his ragtag pirate crew are exemplary of the globalisation of popular culture and protest repertoires, which are no longer shaped exclusively by the West. Even the ubiquity of the three-finger salute drawn from the Hunger Games cannot be reduced to the success of Suzanne Collins’ books and their adaptation for the big screen. The gesture became a symbol of democracy and anti-authoritarian struggles in response to the Thai coup d’état of 2014, before being adopted by Hong Kong protesters the same year and by opponents to the military junta of Myanmar in 2021.

The analogy between the ongoing French student movement and other youthful protests of the past few years should not be overblown, however. In France, unlike in Nepal or Madagascar, the critique of elites has not been focusing on their nepotism but, rather, on their compromising with the capitalist class and the far right. A newly emerged theme, until then reserved to conspiracy theorists leaning to the far right, is that of ‘paedophile elites’ — a theme which seems to have been nurtured by the global scandal of the Epstein files but which has a special resonance among French youths due to the fact that President Emmanuel Macron was only 15 when he met his future wife Brigitte Trogneux, who at the time was 39 years old.

The deeply unpopular president has been a target of much criticism by young protesters. But even though some of them have been asking for his resignation, the movement has not put this demand at the forefront. Protesters do not really have the will — nor the means — to take down the government, the way their counterparts in Bangladesh, Nepal or Madagascar did. And while the government of Sébastien Lecornu was seriously rattled by the scenes of chaos of 17 October, it stood its ground and survived the storm. So far, it has only made minimal concessions to the protesters and does not seem ready to move further due to budgetary constraints. As a result, if some young activists strive to keep the movement afloat, most eyes are now set on the presidential election of April/May 2027, which could bring its own share of civil strife, possibly on an even grander scale.

item.title: Towards stronger ties with Australia. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We are encouraged by the high-level discussions that took place last Sunday between Foreign Secretary Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury and Australian High Commissioner Susan Ryle at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The discussion, centring on trade, investment, energy security, skills development, and labour mobility, signal an encouraging momentum in Dhaka-Canberra relations.
As Bangladesh navigates complex macroeconomic pressures and seeks to diversify its international partnerships, deepening engagement with a major economy like Australia is an opportunity we cannot afford to treat as routine diplomatic pleasantry.
Australia’s historical goodwill toward Bangladesh, dating back to its early recognition of our independence in 1972, is well documented. With that said, diplomatic warmth alone does not generate foreign direct investment, resolve energy deficits, or create jobs.
At this moment in time, attracting credible Australian capital and technical expertise would be of immense value to our economic recovery, as would focusing on education, vocational training, and skilled migration.
With nearly a third of our educated youth facing unemployment while domestic remittances remain a critical pillar of macroeconomic stability, structured mobility pathways and Australian-accredited technical partnerships could transform Bangladesh’s workforce into a competitive global asset.
However, bilateral potential with any and all nations repeatedly stalls when confronted with domestic institutional bottlenecks - and is a reality that we must not just confront but overcome.
Australian investors will not commit long-term capital if they continue to encounter red tape, bureaucratic inertia, energy unreliability, or erratic tax policies.
The government therefore must move swiftly from courtesy calls to concrete, time-bound frameworks. Strengthening ties with Australia is an undeniable positive but the onus is on the government to execute the reforms required to make this partnership truly count.

item.title: Rebalancing the tax burden. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A recent study by the Research and Policy Integration for Development (RAPID) has sparked a necessary debate over fairness in Bangladesh’s fiscal system, finding that the poorest 10% of households pay value-added tax (VAT) equivalent to one-fifth of their reported income compared to just 2.8% for the wealthiest 10%.
As such, while the authors responsibly noted methodological caveats, including the likelihood of income underreporting in household surveys and a more proportionate picture when measured against consumption expenditure, the underlying structural reality remains troubling and one we have known for a long time: Our tax system leans far too heavily on regressive consumption taxes that disproportionately squeeze low-income citizens.
As experts have opined and this newspaper has editorialized numerous times, mobilizing public revenue must go beyond chasing arbitrary collection targets; it must uphold fairness, transparency, and public trust.
Currently, Bangladesh’s tax-to-GDP ratio languishes around 7% -- one of the lowest in the region -- largely because direct taxation remains chronically under-enforced. Despite earning over 40% of total household income and accounting for more than 93% of potential personal income tax, the wealthiest decile largely escapes the net.
Crucially, experts agree that Bangladesh does not need to invent punitive new levies to fix its fiscal deficit. Simply enforcing compliance with existing income tax and domestic VAT laws could be transformative.
While Finance Secretary Md Khairuzzaman Mozumder assuring that the government will examine progressive income tax restructuring, realistic market-based land valuations, and surcharge adjustments to address these issues is a welcome starting point, intent must translate into decisive execution.
An equitable society cannot be built by disproportionately taxing the daily necessities of its poorest citizens while high earners slip through regulatory cracks. True fiscal reform demands shifting the burden so that every citizen contributes in fair proportion to their means.

item.title: Calmer winter seas bring growing fears of human trafficking. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
During a visit to Teknaf last month, I spoke with residents and religious leaders about what worried them as winter approached.
One religious leader feared that calmer seas would make it easier for smugglers and traffickers to launch boats from the Teknaf coast. As we talked, the conversation turned to decisions families face on land.
When work is scarce, a broker’s promise of a job abroad can be hard to turn down. When someone disappears, their family may have no idea where to look or whom to call.
Both concerns surfaced on November 20, 2026, when law enforcement officers rescued 28 people from a trawler that had reached Laboni Point in Cox’s Bazar.
Some survivors said they had been lured with promises of passage to Malaysia. Others said they had been abducted at gunpoint in Teknaf.
Survivors also reported beatings and demands for ransom. Weeks earlier, a ninth-grade student had been abducted, held for weeks and sold from one broker to another before being put aboard a trawler.
His account points to a period when a family’s report could help investigators search for someone on land.
The winter sailing season is a concern for people on shore. The International Organization for Migration says sea crossings typically pick up again in November. Its 2026 assessment warned that worsening conditions in the Cox’s Bazar camps and continued conflict in Myanmar’s Rakhine State could push more Rohingya refugees to attempt the journey.
UNHCR recorded more than 6,500 Rohingya refugees attempting dangerous crossings in 2025, with nearly 900 reported dead or missing in the Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea. Calmer conditions make it easier to set out. The accounts from Laboni Point show the dangers people can face once aboard, whatever brought them there.
For those of us who work with communities, an awareness session should prepare people for a decision they might actually face. At a school assembly, a youth group meeting, or a courtyard discussion with parents, we can walk through a familiar example: A broker offers a job abroad and asks for money that day. Who is the employer? Is there a written contract? Is the recruiter licensed?
Teachers and religious leaders can show families how to check the license in the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training’s register. A short Bangla handout can give families a place to seek advice before paying or handing over documents.
A suspected abduction or confinement calls for urgent action. Humanitarian organi z ations and local police should agree on named police contact for urgent reports and tell families how to follow up.
Community leaders can help families pass on details such as the last known location, the broker’s number or a ransom message directly to police.
In the Rohingya camps, protection teams can offer a confidential way to report threats and help people reach the appropriate authorities. Police should look for links across reports of disappearances, confinement, and ransom demands. A detail from one family may help investigators act on another family’s report.
That cooperation should continue after a rescue. Someone who paid a smuggler to cross a border may have faced threats or exploitation during the journey. Someone else may have been forced aboard from the start.
Police and humanitarian workers should speak with survivors privately and arrange support according to their needs, including medical care, safe contact with family, and specialist referrals for children.
This winter, teachers, religious leaders and humanitarian workers can help families check job offers and know how to report a suspected abduction. When a family raises the alarm, they should have someone they trust to turn to and a clear way to get help while there is still time to search on land.
Md Shihabul Hossain works as Deputy Manager with BRAC Migration Program. The views expressed are personal.

item.title: The middle class is vanishing. Who will rescue them?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For several decades, most Bangladeshis have had the same aspirations. To graduate from university, get a reasonably good job, purchase a home, put your children through higher education in another country, look after your aging parents, and eventually retire with dignity.
We are not dreaming of extravagant wealth here. We are simply dreaming of a level of financial security and stability that we are rapidly losing.
Pay day is followed by one’s obligations to pay the monthly rent, buy groceries, pay school fees, transportation and utility bills, etc. One unexpected major expense (for example, a major medical procedure) can quickly wipe out one’s savings.
Although some families are experiencing an increase in overall income, even for them, after these expenditures are made, they are left with very little, if any, spending money for the month.
Recent World Bank reports indicate that during FY 2026, an additional 2.1 million people are projected to be in poverty. Further, during this same period, the national poverty rate in Bangladesh increased from 18.7% to an estimated 21.4%.
We are now faced with the much greater challenge of keeping previously elevated living standards attained by some of the population from slipping back into poverty.
Meanwhile, for the poorest of the population, increasing costs of production can rapidly change their lives for the worse whereas for the wealthy, such increases may be little more than minor inconveniences.
The average monthly income of urban households (based on the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics’ Living Standard Survey of 2025) is Tk 33,513, and the average monthly expenditure of human households in Bangladesh stands at Tk 35,311 ( an average monthly deficit of Tk 1,798).
During this period, 47% of the households in our survey were reported to have taken out loans to meet their living expenses. These numbers demonstrate the financial challenges faced by families in Bangladesh.
Families may be stretched financially so much that they are unable to purchase school supplies, have no other way of supporting children through education to attain employment, and are thus unable to secure a better future for them.
A part of this salary crisis that has been overlooked is the fact that middle class spending is as much about aspiration as it is about consumption. Middle class parents send their children to better schools in order to create more opportunities for them in the future. They also spend money on coaching to increase their child’s chances of getting through better universities.
Another growing concern for families in Bangladesh is the cost of housing. In Dhaka, for example, to meet monthly expenses, many families have to move to smaller apartments or endure extremely long commutes from workplaces.
While the rent may be low, the opportunity cost ( lost time, stress, and/or distance from schools, hospitals, etc) associated with that location may be quite high.
We believe that with good financial security, middle class households should be able to set aside savings during periods of sickness or unemployment to enable them to educate their children. However, given the ongoing increases in prices, this is becoming increasingly difficult to achieve.
In October 2026, the average nominal wage growth rate (7.63%) was also lower than the general inflation rate (8.27%) indicating that, in real terms, wages decreased during this period. If we assume a household is able to save Tk 10,000 each month, they will still be at a financial loss to meet their monthly expenses if, for example, costs of education and/or health services increase.
Of likely greater concern to most households is the impact of inflation on the family’s ability to save/take out loans to finance larger purchases to ensure they achieve their goal of economic mobility.
Based on current information available to us, any realistic scenario for addressing the current middle class crisis in Bangladesh would need to incorporate measures to improve the overall wage level for the population as a whole, in addition to increasing the level of investment and productivity in the economy.
We understand that the missing middle class in Bangladesh is largely due to the overall economic slowdown. Bangladesh should also be proactive to encourage and empower females to participate in the economy.
It is evident that no single policy will likely result in an immediate transformation. While inflation control is arguably the most important thing we can do now, simply controlling inflation will not solve the situation of the middle class. Further improvements to the economy( better job opportunities, better public health and education facilities, improved public transport, etc) are also needed.
Looking ahead
For decades, the middle class of Bangladesh has lived with a certain promise -- to work hard today to give his children an easier future.
A father delays purchasing his own house to pay for his children’s education. A mother deprives herself of the ordinary pleasures of life in order to save up for her children. A young man works overtime every week in the vain hope that one day, his family will not have to count every single taka to determine whether they will be able to make it through this month.
What happens to this family when the sudden need for additional expenses exhausts their accumulated savings? When they realize that no amount of additional work will improve their situation? When they begin to believe that their children will not have a better life than they did?
These are the true tragedies of a diminishing middle class. It’s not just losing your means of economic survival. It means slowly losing hope for the future.
We must do all we can to preserve hope, especially among the millions of families that struggle to just get by. All they have ever wanted is the right to live and to be able to dream of a better future for their families.
If in the future, we look back on the development of Bangladesh and are unable to find sufficient examples of fathers and mothers being able to rest easy at night, knowing their family is safe and secure, then we should question how prosperous our country really is.
Yemad Fayed is a PR professional.

item.title: Can Bangladesh turn its hard-won progress into lasting strength?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Over the past four decades, Bangladesh has undergone a substantial economic transformation. From a predominantly agrarian economy marked by widespread poverty, the nation has built a robust manufacturing and export infrastructure, significantly increased remittance inflows, and improved key human development indicators. Notably, the ready-made garment (RMG) sector has emerged as a significant player on the global stage.
However, economic resilience goes beyond endurance during adverse conditions; it reflects an economy's capacity to absorb shocks, recover quickly, and adapt effectively while safeguarding the welfare of its populace. For Bangladesh, this paradigm has become increasingly critical as it confronts a range of challenges, including persistent inflation, financial-sector vulnerabilities, insufficient investment, climate change-related risks, geopolitical volatility, and the complex imperative of advancing beyond its current status as a least-developed country (LDC).
Again, while Bangladesh is classified as a least developed country, academic discourse offers different views on whether the government of Bangladesh should keep or change its status. The biggest LDC benefits for Bangladesh have been:
Bangladesh's status as an LDC has facilitated export-led growth, particularly in the RMG sector, but has also led to a reliance on external trade benefits. This dependency poses challenges, as Bangladesh must move beyond preferential treatment and focus on productivity, innovation, and diversification.
To maintain its global standing as a productive, independent economy, Bangladesh must strengthen competitiveness. Consequently, Bangladesh should analyze its LDC graduation with a focus on socio-economic and political factors to build a sustainable competitive framework post-graduation.
The World Bank indicates that the immediate economic forecast for Bangladesh is still uncertain, with GDP growth anticipated to be 3.9% for FY2026. This prediction comes amid persistent inflation, rising poverty, and significant pressure on the banking sector, requiring strategic action to strengthen economic stability and support continued growth.
The nation averaged about 6% annual GDP growth over the last decade. As the country's largest export-driven sector, the RMG industry is crucial but vulnerable because it relies heavily on a single industry. According to the World Trade Organization, garments make up about 81% to 84% of Bangladesh's merchandise exports, ranking the sector among the most vital sources of foreign currency and jobs in the country. More than half of the roughly 4.5 million workers in this sector are women.
Remittances also serve as an essential safety net. Bangladeshis employed abroad remit billions of dollars home each year, supporting household spending and foreign-exchange availability. These trends suggest Bangladesh's resilience does not rely on a single institution or policy; instead, it has developed through a mix of export manufacturing, overseas employment, agriculture, local entrepreneurship, women’s workforce participation, and a robust domestic market.

Bangladesh's export achievements have been modest, but reliance on a single sector adds risk. The garment sector accounts for most merchandise exports, with primary markets in the European Union and the United States. According to the WTO, about 40% of Bangladesh’s garment exports went to the EU and 18% to the US in 2024.
This focus makes Bangladesh vulnerable to fluctuations in global consumer trends, trade regulations, supply chains, labour standards, and environmental expectations. The country's anticipated transition from least-developed-country (LDC) status signifies a significant challenge.
While graduation is a noteworthy achievement, some trade benefits linked to LDC status will eventually change. The WTO highlights that the Bangladeshi business community is particularly worried about sustaining market access and complying with stricter rules of origin.
Thus, for Bangladesh, building economic resilience increasingly means shifting from low-cost competitiveness to improving productivity, quality, technology, and skills, and diversifying exports.
Bangladesh's economy has become increasingly vulnerable to global political and economic disturbances because it relies on imported energy, export markets, remittances, global supply chains, and foreign currency. The World Bank stresses the urgent need for policy reforms to reestablish macroeconomic stability, boost revenue collection, fortify the financial sector, and improve the business climate to encourage job creation and inclusive growth. Many low-income workers continue to struggle with stagnant wages that erode their purchasing power.
While external pressures eased in FY25 and early FY26 due to strong remittance flows and a more adaptable exchange rate, financial sector vulnerabilities remain elevated, with a non-performing loan ratio of over 30%. Small and medium-sized enterprises face considerable challenges, including high regulatory costs and inadequate infrastructure, underscoring the need for targeted deregulation and stronger competition policies to promote private sector development.
In Bangladesh, the primary focus tends to be on real GDP growth rather than the future dollar value of GDP. Variations are significant because different institutions use different forecast dates, assumptions, and models.
The IMF's January 2026 forecast estimated growth of 4.7% for both FY2026 and FY2027, but its July 2026 staff assessment later revised FY2027 growth to 3.5%, showing how forecasts can shift as conditions change.
The ADB's September 2026 outlook maintained its growth projection for Bangladesh at 3.7% for FY2026. The World Bank's most recent country outlook for Bangladesh projects growth of 3.9% in FY2026, rising gradually to 5.3% by FY2028.
Another dimension Bangladesh cannot afford to overlook is climate change.
Bangladesh is highly exposed to floods, cyclones, river erosion, salinity, and other climate-related hazards. These are not merely environmental problems. They can destroy infrastructure, reduce agricultural production, displace workers, and increase government expenditure.
The IMF has identified building resilience to natural disasters as a major priority for Bangladesh and has called for climate-resilient infrastructure and greater access to climate finance.
This makes Bangladesh an important example of why economic resilience and climate resilience are increasingly inseparable.
Perhaps the most important question is not simply whether Bangladesh's GDP can recover. It is who benefits from recovery.
A resilient economy should protect vulnerable households while creating opportunities for workers, entrepreneurs and young people. Recent data indicate that Bangladesh has faced declining labour-force participation, with women disproportionately affected.
The World Bank reported that labour-force participation fell from 60.9% to 58.9% between 2023 and 2024, while women accounted for 2.4 million of the additional three million working-age people outside the labour force.
This suggests that resilience needs to include employment resilience.
Bangladesh's large young population can be a demographic advantage if workers receive appropriate education, digital skills, technical training, and access to productive employment. Conversely, insufficient job creation could turn demographic potential into economic pressure.
Small and medium-sized enterprises also deserve particular attention. The World Bank notes that many SMEs face regulatory costs, unreliable infrastructure and limited access to finance.
A resilient Bangladesh cannot depend exclusively on large garment exporters. It needs a broader ecosystem of competitive firms across manufacturing, agriculture, pharmaceuticals, information technology, logistics, tourism, financial services and other knowledge-intensive sectors.
The economic history of Bangladesh offers a crucial insight: Resilience does not mean dodging every crisis. Every economy faces challenges. Instead, resilience requires the institutions, capabilities, and social frameworks needed to endure disruptions and come back stronger.
Despite exploitation discourse, Bangladesh has already proven its ability to adapt and evolve in the garment industry; increased overseas employment, rising remittances, and advances in the agricultural sector, with minimal human development, show that adaptation is achievable.
Corruption, political instability, and lack of social justice can seriously obstruct Bangladesh's ability to convert economic growth into widespread, sustainable advancement. Corruption can misappropriate public funds, undermine institutions, deter investment, and diminish the efficiency of public services. Political instability and uncertainty can disrupt policy-making, erode investor confidence, and delay essential economic and institutional reforms.
Additionally, a lack of social justice -- evidenced by unequal access to education, healthcare, job opportunities, and legal protections -- can marginalize disadvantaged groups and exacerbate social inequality. Together, these issues can erode public trust and institutional effectiveness, constraining Bangladesh’s ability to turn its economic potential into inclusive development and higher living standards.
The World Bank warns that without structural changes in revenue generation, the financial sector, and the business environment, Bangladesh's previous resilience could wane. The IMF supports this view, saying reforms are crucial to restore macroeconomic stability and promote long-term development.
For Bangladesh, the key economic challenge is transformation. It is no longer simply about rapid growth; it now involves building an economy that can sustain prosperity amid evolving global trade dynamics, worsening climate challenges, technological shifts in employment, and the declining reliability of traditional competitive strengths.
The country's next development phase may depend on its ability to shift resilience from merely enduring shocks to consistently adapting and creating new opportunities.
This transition would redefine economic resilience not merely as a response to crises, but as a core component of Bangladesh's long-term growth strategy.
Dr ASM Anam Ullah (PhD) is an Australian senior academic, editor, human rights activist, political and economic analyst, and OHS and industrial relations expert.

item.title: We are losing the fight against dengue. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
With 518 confirmed deaths as of writing this editorial and fast approaching 175,000 hospitalizations recorded so far this year, marking the third-deadliest outbreak in Bangladesh’s history, our response to dengue remains inadequate, to say the least.
Why such a response has descended from disappointing to outright infuriating is because three years after the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) drafted the National Dengue Prevention and Control Strategy (2024-2030), virtually zero tangible progress is visible on the ground.
Dengue has long been far more than an unpredictable seasonal anomaly and rather an annual public health emergency. Yet, the battle against dengue is one Bangladesh continues to lose because of chronic administrative incompetence.
As prominent entomologists and public health experts have rightly pointed out, the national strategy itself is fundamentally flawed, allegedly drafted behind closed doors by bureaucrats without input from entomologists or field specialists, rendering it unscientific and detached from reality.
Worse still, even the basic directives within that document remain unexecuted. Year-round destruction of Aedes breeding grounds is nonexistent, coordination between the health ministry and local government bodies remains broken, and disease surveillance misses countless cases treated or lost at home.
Equally inexcusable is the continued centralization of treatment. By failing to equip district and upazila hospitals with adequate diagnostic kits, skilled personnel, and intensive care capacity, authorities force critically ill patients from across the country to undertake perilous journeys to Dhaka, overwhelming capital hospitals.
Bureaucratic inertia continues costing innocent citizens their lives. If the government wants to demonstrate that it truly cares about people’s suffering, then it must immediately overhaul its failed approach. We cannot keep treating preventable deaths as inevitable statistics.

item.title: Execution is everything for development projects. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The 16 recent development projects approved by the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (Ecnec) worth Tk33,298.48 crore, of which less than Tk500cr will be from external sources, is certainly an ambitious push to strengthen rural connectivity, revive dying waterways, and bolster agricultural productivity.
From constructing 256 long rural bridges to excavating nearly 8,900 kilometres of canals, small rivers, and waterbodies across 444 upazilas, we can admire the scope and scale of these initiatives and can recognize that they target genuine developmental needs.
Building pillar-free bridges that protect natural river flows while linking remote communities, alongside restoring surface water irrigation across 2.65 lakh hectares of farmland, could deliver lasting economic and ecological dividends. These are interventions that are necessary for future prosperity.
With that said, Bangladesh’s development landscape is full of well-intentioned infrastructure schemes ruined by bad planning and worse implementation as a result of corrupt practices.
At a moment when public finances are stretched razor-thin amid severe revenue shortfalls, high inflation, and mounting debt obligations, every single taka is precious. As such, we have zero margin for waste, vanity spending, or bureaucratic lethargy.
Equally important is ensuring full safety before the project is greenlit for the implementation stage. To that end, that there remain dozens of bridges which still have not undergone feasibility studies does not inspire confidence, and must be addressed promptly. Approving massive construction packages before completing rigorous hydrological surveys and engineering assessments is a recipe for disaster.
If these projects are to succeed, the government must enforce ironclad fiscal and operational discipline from day one. Beyond ensuring the bridges requiring feasibility studies undergo thorough, independent technical evaluations, strict timelines and fixed budget ceilings must be enforced, along with penalties for contractors and project directors who manufacture artificial delays to inflate costs.
Approving projects has always merely been the starting line. It is disciplined, corruption-free execution that has eluded us.

item.title: School should be the safest space for every learner. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A mocking laugh in class, a hurtful message forwarded online or silence when a classmate is harassed can make students afraid to return to school. Every child in Bangladesh has the right to walk through the school gate free from fear. Protecting that right takes work throughout the school year. Every secondary school should have trained staff, clear procedures to prevent violence, and respond when students report it.
Globally, about one in three students reports being bullied. Estimates put the share of children affected by cyberbullying at around one in ten . Harm can be amplified online through image-based abuse and sexual extortion. Girls and boys can face different forms of violence, and poverty and disability can increase the risks. Fear can make it harder for students to learn even when they are in class.
Bangladesh has made gains in girls’ enrolment. Today, girls are enrolling in secondary schools at higher rates than boys. Yet many leave before completing Grade 10 .
The latest 2022 Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey found that about half of women aged 20 to 24 years had married before the age of 18. In the most recent 2024 Violence Against Women Survey , about 62% of ever-married girls aged 15 to 19 years reported experiencing intimate partner violence in the preceding year. Schools and communities both have a role in addressing the pressures girls face beyond the classroom.
A situation analysis on Health Promoting Schools , published in 2026 by the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE) with Unesco’s support, surveyed 458 students and 206 teachers across the country. Only 30.1% of teachers reported having received training in health education or well-being.
The study suggested that health topics receive limited classroom time partly because they are not examined. Schools can build on that support by involving families in work on safety and well-being.
The Health Promoting Schools approach makes health and well-being part of how schools teach and operate. By 2021, more than 90 countries and territories had adopted the initiative and the global Health Promoting Schools (HPS) standards and indicators published by WHO and Unesco.
Unesco’s Education for Health and Well-being strategy links healthy school systems with age-appropriate life skills and health education with learning environments free from violence and bullying. The 2023 Unesco Recommendation on Education for Peace, Human Rights and Sustainable Development identifies the safety, health, and well-being of learners and education personnel as a guiding principle. It calls for strengthening the school system to support students’ physical and mental health.
Since 2024, DSHE and the National Academy for Educational Management (NAEM), with Unesco’s support, have been piloting HPS in 30 schools in urban and rural areas of Bangladesh. The pilot has generated evidence, adapted the standards and indicators for Bangladesh and developed a competency-based curriculum for teachers, delivered through master trainers. Alongside DSHE’s Learning Acceleration in Secondary Education (LAISE) project and its cyberbullying training, it has supported reporting through complaint boxes and school anti-sexual harassment committees.
We call on government, development partners, and communities to extend this work to every secondary school, starting where need is greatest. The Health Promoting Schools standards adapted for Bangladesh can serve as a national benchmark. Each school should have a code of conduct, a complaint box, and a committee responsible for school safety.
A complaint box gives a student a way to speak up. What happens after a report determines whether that student gets help. Schools should be able to refer students confidentially to health, psychosocial, social, and legal services.
Education, health, social welfare, and law enforcement agencies should plan together so schools know where to turn. Union parishads and upazilas can help make school surroundings safer.
Teacher training should cover the skills set out in the HPS approach, including positive discipline and digital safety. Prioritize government and rural schools, where the study found teachers had received less training.
The curriculum and textbooks should teach students how to recognize and respond to online abuse, protect their privacy, and use the internet responsibly. Parents and teachers need these skills too, so they can support children when harm occurs online.
Families, religious and community leaders, and young people have a role in changing the norms that sustain child marriage. When a girl or boy drops out, schools and communities should follow up and help that learner return.
Schools should assess safety each year, plan and carry out improvements, then monitor and review progress. They should track violence, attendance, and dropout alongside the HPS indicators and learning outcomes. Pilot schools can share what works, and the findings can inform Bangladesh’s reporting under Unesco’s 2023 Recommendation.
Bangladesh’s promise of an education for every child must be kept in the classroom, on the way to school and in the online spaces children use. When a student can speak up about harm, receive support, and return to learning in safety, that promise is being put into practice.
Professor Dr Khan Moinuddin Al Mahmud Sohel , Director General, Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education. Professor Dr Wasim Md Mazbahul Haque , Director General, National Academy for Educational Management. Dr Susan Vize, Head of Office and Unesco Representative to Bangladesh.

item.title: Why cancel culture will never stick in Bangladesh. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Walk past any cha-er dokan in Dhaka on a humid evening and you will witness the true theatre of Bangladeshi public opinion.
One week, the table is united in righteous fury over a global brand, a viral clip, or a celebrity’s court-premises clash.
Voices rise, thumbs fly across cracked screens, and solemn pledges of permanent ostracization are made.
Two weeks later, the exact same crowd is arguing about cricket selections, inflation, or the next three-second clip to cross their feeds, reaching without a second thought for whatever they had just sworn off.
Cancel culture -- that distinctly Western export built on moral registries, algorithmic pile-ons, and long-memoried corporate or career exile -- never quite survives the journey to Bangladesh.
Not because Bangladeshis lack passion. Quite the opposite: We have passion in industrial quantities.
The problem is our attention span, our social fabric, and a deeply ingrained cultural habit of moving on before the kettle has even stopped whistling.
The anatomy of a thirty-day boycott
Consider the wave of consumer anger directed at Coca-Cola in Bangladesh following the escalation of the Gaza war and the backlash over its local advertising missteps.
For a stretch, boycotting multinational brands felt like a moral badge worn across timelines, with local alternatives like Mojo and RC Cola enjoying a visible surge of patriotic goodwill.
Yet retail realities in Bangladesh are notoriously stubborn.
Convenience, price points, distribution muscle, and sheer habit have a way of eroding ideological resolutions once the peak of a news cycle passes.
Even when a campaign dents sales or forces a PR scramble, turning a burst of moral indignation into permanent market erasure requires sustained discipline -- something mass outrage rarely maintains once life’s daily pressures resume.
The same short half-life shows up in celebrity and media flashpoints. Take the recurring storm around actress Pori Moni and her volatile clashes with journalists -- from heated exchanges and allegations of phone-snatching around court appearances to live-streamed accusations of "terrorism in the name of journalism."
Journalists’ associations have called protests or boycotts, commentators have dissected every angle, and social media has briefly crowned winners and villains.
Yet in Bangladesh’s entertainment and tabloid ecosystem, outrage and publicity are often Siamese twins.
A figure who is "cancelled" in one clip can re-emerge in another viral moment days later, carried forward by the very curiosity that fuelled the condemnation.
From 1990s print panics to 2020s timeline storms
Fickleness is not a gift bestowed solely on smartphones; it is an old habit wearing new clothes.
In the 1990s, as private newspapers, FM radio, and satellite television began opening up Bangladesh’s media landscape, public panics and moral outrages already moved in brisk cycles -- whether around sensational crime coverage, shifting political slogans, or cultural debates over foreign television and music.
Back then, distance and slower print cycles meant a controversy had to work harder to travel, and once the next edition hit the stands, yesterday’s scandal was already losing oxygen.
By the 2010s and 2020s, Facebook and short-form video turned that slow burn into instant wildfire.
Over the last decade and a half, Bangladesh has seen countless online storms: Sudden boycotts of specific TV dramas or advertisers, fierce pile-ons against influencers and public figures, and rapid shifts in what the entire nation is "definitely not watching or buying anymore."
History has shown that social media in Bangladesh can power massive real-world mobilization when grievances run deep and structural -- as seen during the student-led anti-discrimination uprising -- but ordinary cultural "cancelling" rarely holds.
Most online boycotts here behave less like court sentences and more like monsoon rain: Loud, dramatic, impossible to ignore for an hour, and quickly soaked into the pavement.
Across borders and back home
Zoom out across South Asia and the wider world, and you see why this pattern looks so familiar. Across South Asia, Bollywood and regional film industries have repeatedly faced hashtag boycotts -- sometimes hurting an opening weekend or two, only for audiences to return whenever a film’s buzz or star power hits the right chord.
In the West, where cancel culture is often treated as an inescapable social guillotine, even high-profile cancellations frequently turn out to be porous: Audiences split, algorithms move on to fresh targets, and figures with loyal niches often claw back visibility or reinvent themselves.
If cancel culture struggles to stay rigid even in societies built around individualist branding and HR-style accountability, it stands even less chance in Bangladesh.
Western cancel culture thrives on a tidy moral ledger: You cross a line, the crowd withdraws its patronage, and institutions enforce the exile.
Bangladesh does not run on tidy ledgers.
Our social life is dense, relational, and forgiving in ways that are both generous and frustrating.
Personal ties, addas , kinship networks, political alignments, and economic survival constantly cut across neat moral lines.
What looks like an unbreakable boycott on a Monday morning often dissolves into pragmatism -- or plain boredom -- by Friday afternoon.
Why we never quite stay mad
There is also a quieter truth behind our fickle-mindedness: Living in Bangladesh already demands a high daily quota of outrage.
Between traffic, rising living costs, workplace stress, and constant political or civic noise, nobody has the emotional bandwidth to stay furious at a soda brand or an actress’s press-scrum temper forever.
None of this means public criticism in Bangladesh is pointless.
Calling out bad ads, holding public figures accountable, or questioning corporate behaviour matters when it sparks real debate.
But expecting a Western-style cancel culture to permanently erase people or products in Bangladesh is misreading the room.
Here, the crowd rarely holds a grudge long enough to finish the sentence -- because by then, another notification has already lit up the screen.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.
