item.title: How ancient philosophy became modern self-help. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
"O jar apon khobor apnar hoy na
ekbar apnare chinte parle re jabe achenare chena.”
In other words, someone who does not know their own self may come to know what once seemed unknown by learning who they really are.
Lalon Fakir sang those lines in Kushtia, in a mud hut, without formal schooling or scripture to guide him, and without any apparent need to convince anyone of anything. He was not setting out to write philosophy. He was putting an insight into words, as village songs often do, and somehow arrived at something a Roman emperor would write down in a war tent and a Greek slave who became a teacher would repeat to his students: Know yourself first, and the rest begins to make sense.
That, really, is what this article is about. We tend to think that wisdom about how to live is something new, something we find in a bestselling book or pick up from a fifteen-minute TED Talk. But most of these questions are much older than the labels we give them.
Bauls sang about them on the roads of Kushtia, philosophers debated them in gardens outside Athens, and an emperor wrote about them between battles, long before anyone thought to call this kind of advice “self-help.”
Mark Manson makes a similar point in his essay “Why We All Need Philosophy,” where he argues that we need a way of thinking suited to the problems of modern life. Look closely at today’s self-help culture and you can see what he means: It often circles back to conclusions philosophers reached thousands of years ago, only with better marketing.
Take Cal Newport’s Deep Work , which urges us to protect our attention from distraction. Seneca was making a related point long ago when he observed that people guard their money carefully but throw away their time, “the one thing in which it is right to be stingy,” as though it costs them nothing.
James Clear’s Atomic Habits makes the case that our identity shapes our behaviour. Epictetus had already put the idea plainly: “First say to yourself what you would be; and then do what you have to do.”
Sharon Lebell brings the same spirit to The Art of Living: The Classical Manual on Virtue, Happiness, and Effectiveness , her modern rendering of Epictetus. At the heart of the Stoic teaching is a simple distinction: Some things are within our control, and some are not. Much of our suffering begins when we fail to tell the difference.
That idea was written down when Rome was still an empire. Today, it sits close to the heart of an industry that sells us advice on how to live.
Living in the age of statistics
Today, almost everything can be tracked, measured, optimized, or tested against something else.
We know our sleep scores, our step counts, and how many minutes we have spent looking at a screen. We can measure a remarkable amount about our lives, sometimes down to the smallest detail. And yet all that information does not necessarily tell us whether we are living well. For all the numbers we collect, many of us still feel unsure about where we are going.
Compare that with the philosophers of antiquity. They did not have our devices or data, but they spent a great deal of time asking a question we still struggle with: What does it actually mean to live well?
Epicurus, who is often mistaken for a champion of indulgence, argued for something closer to radical simplicity. He wrote: “It is possible to provide security against other ills, but as far as death is concerned, we men live in a city without walls.”
He was not asking people to outrun death by staying busy or gathering more possessions. He was asking them to look clearly at what matters and what does not.
“If you wish to be rich, do not add to your money, but subtract from your desires.” It is hard to think of a more direct challenge to a culture that keeps telling us we need one more thing before we can be satisfied.
What the ancients knew that we keep relearning
A few ideas recur across the schools of ancient philosophy, and they sound remarkably familiar beside the advice filling the self-improvement shelves today.
Marcus Aurelius, the philosopher-emperor, wrote what could almost pass for an early productivity mantra: “You have power over your mind -- not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.”
Long before Deep Work , the underlying point was already there: You cannot control everything happening around you, but you can pay attention to how you respond.
Seneca argued that a life without hardship leaves a person untested. He compared it to a fighter who has never taken a real hit. What we now call grit, he understood as a part of character: something that is formed, in part, by having to face difficulty.
Epictetus put it this way: “Make the best use of what is in your power, and take the rest as it happens.” The idea resembles what we now call locus of control: Knowing where your effort can make a difference, and learning not to spend all your energy on what lies beyond it.
None of these similarities is especially surprising. Our tools have changed far more than our basic human worries. We have built rockets and neural networks, but we still wake up anxious about things we cannot control.
And we still need someone, whether a Stoic teacher who was once enslaved or a productivity YouTuber, to remind us to sit down and do the next right thing.
Philosophy is not complicated
Somewhere along the way, philosophy became a university subject rather than a way of living. It was wrapped in dense texts, footnotes, and academic language, then put behind the doors of departments that often struggle to attract students.
Philosophy was never meant to stay inside a lecture hall. It belongs in that brief moment before you lose your temper and say something you cannot take back.
Epictetus made much the same point to his students nearly 2,000 years ago. For him, philosophy was not something to admire from a distance. He urged his followers not to stop at learning, but to put what they learned into practice and keep training themselves.
Returning to the question
We live in a culture that measures value by output. Time is something to spend efficiently, a person is something to optimize, and even learning is treated as an investment that must pay a return. In this logic, a question earns its place only if it produces something.
Questions that cannot be priced, such as what makes a life good or what we owe one another, do not disappear. They simply lose their place, or never occur to us at all, because the world gives us no reason to look for them.
What follows is a habit of passive consumption. We take in advice, trends, and ready-made formulas for success, and we rarely stop to examine them. The meaning of a good life is defined for us by markets, media, and the people around us, and we adopt it without asking whether it is ours.
Philosophy was not refuted. It was crowded out by busyness, and by the belief that reflection is a luxury for when the work is done. Epicurus warned against dismissing philosophy in just this way:
“He who says either that the time for philosophy has not yet come or that it has passed is like someone who says that the time for happiness has not yet come or that it has passed.”
The self-help industry is not wrong to return to habits, focus, resilience, and meaning. The problem is that it can make old questions look like brand-new discoveries.
Perhaps the next step is not to buy another book, but to return to a practice that the Stoics made time for at the end of the day: Asking yourself what you did well and what you could do better.
Not to punish yourself for getting things wrong, but to learn. You would practice any skill you wanted to improve, so why should living well be any different?
Sharif Al Zubayer Zishan is an aspiring writer and journalist.

item.title: Turning down the noise. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We appreciate the High Court Division issuing a set of interim directives to curb noise pollution in the capital -- ordering regular drives in silent zones, strict regulation of unnecessary honking, and the creation of a dedicated complaint hotline.
It is safe to say, however, that given the authorities' chronic failure to enforce existing noise laws, these latest directives only have meaning should they see implementation.
For the tens of millions of residents of Dhaka, which is routinely ranked the most noise-polluted city on Earth, having meaningful judicial intervention is long overdue.
Every day, citizens endure an unrelenting acoustic assault, from illegal hydraulic horns, unregulated construction, and blaring loudspeakers. Even designated silent zones -- within 100 metres of hospitals, schools, and courts, as well as around Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport and the Secretariat -- remain completely indistinguishable from chaotic traffic intersections.
Bangladesh has never suffered from a shortage of laws or court orders; it suffers from a terminal paralysis of enforcement.
Regulators have long been armed with clear mandates but what has been missing is institutional will. Too often, enforcement amounts to theatrical, one-day mobile court drives for television cameras, followed immediately by business as usual.
The High Court's requirement that relevant ministries and agencies submit compliance reports every three months provides a crucial accountability mechanism, and it must be taken seriously. Judicial directives only matter when backed by relentless, everyday execution.
Dhaka continues to rank near the bottom of global liveability indexes, and its noise pollution is a major reason for this. The citizens of the capital have a right to peace, health, and sanity, and curbing our noise pollution levels is one way to move in the right direction.

item.title: Law enforcement requires genuine reform. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We are sceptical about the latest wave of administrative changes -- including the abrupt transfer of five senior officials in Gopalganj following violent unrest, the relocation of 100 police personnel from Cox's Bazar over alleged narcotics links, and the withdrawal of Chuadanga’s deputy commissioner -- that have once again placed Bangladesh’s law enforcement and civil administration under intense public scrutiny.
While the authorities concerned frame these moves as routine oversight and accountability, senior analysts and legal experts have rightly warned that knee-jerk transfers, forced retirements, and ad-hoc reappointments are not substitutes for genuine institutional reform.
For decades, this country’s policing apparatus has been hollowed out by deep-seated institutional rot, partisan instrumentalization, and a pervasive culture of impunity.
Simply shuffling officers from one district to another when security lapses occur does nothing to fix the wave of systemic failures. Indeed, all it does is merely export incompetence or misconduct to a new area.
Worse still, relying on opaque withdrawals and arbitrary sackings without transparent, evidence-based inquiries breeds fear, paralysis, and mistrust, leaving honest officers hesitant to act decisively.
To describe rampant corruption, intelligence failures, and violent breakdowns in law and order as mere "isolated incidents" is also an exercise in dangerous denial.
Cosmetic reshuffles and intensified internal surveillance cannot cure a force still governed by an archaic, colonial-era command structure that prioritizes political obedience over public service.
If the government is serious about restoring public trust and building a professional, dependable police force, it must abandon reactive firefighting and execute structural overhaul.
Transparency has never been a word associated with our law enforcement nor the government itself, but it is what is needed if we are to see any meaningful change.

item.title: When books disappear, intolerance takes over. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A society does not become chaotic overnight. Its descent into intolerance, hostility, and disorder often begins much earlier, through small but consequential changes in the way people think, communicate, and understand one another.
One such change is the gradual disappearance of the habit of reading. In Bangladesh, where political disagreements increasingly turn into personal hostility, differences of opinion become grounds for confrontation, and public discussions frequently collapse into accusations and counteraccusations, the declining culture of reading deserves far more attention than it receives.
The absence of books from everyday life is not merely an educational deficiency or a cultural inconvenience. It can become a serious social and political liability.
Reading is often treated as an individual intellectual exercise, something people pursue for academic achievement, professional development, or personal entertainment. Yet its social significance extends considerably further.
Books expose readers to unfamiliar experiences, competing arguments, historical realities, and moral complexities. They encourage people to remain with an idea long enough to understand it before accepting or rejecting it.
A society that gradually loses this capacity risks producing citizens who are increasingly confident in their opinions but progressively less capable of examining them. The consequences become visible not only in classrooms but also in families, workplaces, political institutions, and public spaces.
Consider the difference between encountering an argument through a book and encountering it through a social media post. The former generally demands patience, concentration, and engagement with an extended line of reasoning. The latter often delivers conclusions without context, rewards immediate reactions, and encourages emotional identification with particular positions.
Neither medium is inherently incapable of informing people, but their effects depend considerably on how they are used. When short-form digital content becomes the principal source of knowledge, people may gradually lose the patience required to distinguish between evidence, interpretation, speculation, and manipulation.
Complex social problems are consequently reduced to simplistic explanations, while complicated human disagreements become contests between supposedly good and evil individuals.
This intellectual impatience has serious implications for a country like Bangladesh, where political and social divisions are already deeply embedded in public life.
Disagreement is a natural feature of any democratic society. Indeed, democracy cannot function without disagreement. The problem begins when people lose the ability to accept that someone can hold a different opinion without necessarily being ignorant, immoral, or hostile.
Reading literature, history, philosophy, and political thought can help cultivate precisely this understanding. By introducing readers to different historical periods, cultures, ideologies, and human experiences, books challenge the assumption that one's own perspective represents the entirety of reality.
John Stuart Mill, in On Liberty , defended the importance of allowing competing opinions to confront one another because even an erroneous opinion could contain part of the truth. His argument remains particularly relevant in a society where disagreement is frequently interpreted as disloyalty.
A reading culture does not automatically produce tolerant citizens, but it creates opportunities to encounter arguments that challenge existing beliefs. Without such encounters, convictions can harden into unquestionable assumptions, and public discourse can become increasingly hostile.
The relationship between reading and social acceptance is equally important. Literature allows individuals to enter lives vastly different from their own. A reader can experience the anxieties of a marginali z ed person, the desperation of someone living in poverty, the dilemmas of a political dissident, or the frustrations of an individual belonging to an unfamiliar community.
This imaginative engagement does not guarantee empathy, but it expands the possibility of understanding. As Atticus Finch observes in Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird , one cannot truly understand another person without considering things from their perspective. The literary lesson is simple but profound: A cceptance begins when people become willing to imagine experiences beyond their immediate surroundings.
Bangladesh's declining interest in recreational reading should therefore concern us beyond the boundaries of education policy. A January 2025 study, Recreational Book Reading Among Secondary School Students in Bangladesh: Access, Trends and Issues , found that although 87% of participating students considered leisure reading important, only 38% actually read books outside their textbooks.
Another international survey published by CEOWorld Magazine in 2024 placed Bangladesh 97th among 102 countries in reading habits, estimating an average of 2.75 books per person annually.
These figures should be interpreted with an understanding of their methodological limitations, but they nevertheless raise important questions about the country's relationship with books.
The problem is not simply that young people are reading fewer novels or storybooks. It is that the educational environment often teaches them to regard knowledge as something to be acquired for examinations rather than explored for intellectual satisfaction.
A student who spends years memori z ing information without developing curiosity may eventually become a graduate who possesses certificates but struggles to engage critically with unfamiliar ideas. When education becomes primarily a process of reproducing approved answers, independent thinking becomes an unintended casualty.
The consequences can be particularly damaging in the political sphere. Political manipulation thrives where people lack the habit of questioning information, examining historical contexts, and evaluating competing claims. An uninformed public is not necessarily an unintelligent public, but it can become more vulnerable to deliberate misinformation.
When political narratives are consumed without scrutiny, rumours acquire the appearance of facts and collective anger can be directed towards convenient targets. The distance between disagreement and hostility consequently becomes dangerously short.
Gustave Le Bon's The Crowd: A Study of the Popular Mind examined how individual reasoning can become submerged in collective emotional behaviour. Although his arguments should not be treated as a complete explanation of contemporary mass psychology, they offer a useful reminder that crowds can become susceptible to suggestion and emotional contagion.
In Bangladesh, where social media can transform an allegation into a nationwide controversy within hours, the ability to pause, verify, and think independently is an essential civic responsibility. Reading cannot eliminate mob behaviour, but an intellectually curious population is better equipped to question the narratives that provoke it.
There is another dimension to this crisis: T he declining capacity to resolve conflicts through language. Reading develops vocabulary, but its deeper contribution is the ability to articulate disagreement without immediately resorting to aggression.
People who encounter diverse arguments and literary representations of human conflict become familiar with the possibility that opposing positions can contain legitimate concerns. They learn that persuasion requires more than volume, authority, or intimidation. In a society where public arguments increasingly resemble verbal combat, the ability to express disagreement constructively is itself a form of social capital.
Albert Camus, in The Plague , explores how ordinary people respond to collective suffering and moral responsibility. The novel reminds readers that social crises are not overcome through slogans or declarations of righteousness but through sustained responsibility towards others.
Such literature can help cultivate a moral imagination that extends beyond personal interests and political affiliations. This is particularly important in Bangladesh, where the language of collective welfare is frequently invoked but the practi c e of respecting differences remains inconsistent.
Of course, it would be simplistic to blame the country's social tensions entirely on declining reading habits. Economic inequality, unemployment, institutional weaknesses, political polari z ation, inadequate education, and the erosion of public trust all contribute to instability.
Nor does reading necessarily make someone compassionate or morally responsible. History contains enough examples of educated individuals participating in oppression and violence. Books can be misused, selectively interpreted, or turned into instruments of ideological indoctrination.
The real issue, therefore, is not merely how many books people read but whether society encourages independent, critical, and reflective engagement with knowledge.
That responsibility cannot rest exclusively on individuals. Families must create environments where children encounter books as sources of pleasure rather than additional academic burdens. Educational institutions need to move beyond examination-centred instruction and introduce meaningful reading programmes.
The state and local governments should consider public libraries, affordable books, and neighbourhood reading initiatives essential investments in social development. Publishers, writers, and educational institutions also have a responsibility to make books more accessible to readers throughout the year rather than depending excessively on the annual book fair.
A reading culture is not simply about producing more writers, academics, or literary enthusiasts. It is about developing citizens capable of thinking beyond immediate emotions, recogni z ing the humanity of people with whom they disagree, and questioning the assumptions that shape their understanding of the world.
A society that does not read may still produce graduates, professionals, and political leaders, but it risks losing the intellectual resources necessary to sustain meaningful coexistence.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst. Currently he is teaching at IUBAT.

item.title: Who looks after the children of the industrial communities?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Every day, parents across Bangladesh’s industrial hubs leave home to work in factories. For those with young children, one of the daily challenges is finding a safe place for their children to stay while they are at work.
For a young child, a parent’s long working day can mean staying with an older sibling, a relative or another informal caregiver, sometimes without adequate adult supervision.
Parents carry this worry with them to work, knowing that their children may not have access to the care and support they need. For children, the consequences can extend beyond safety to missed opportunities for early learning and greater exposure to other risks.
Bangladesh has invested heavily in industrial infrastructure over the past few decades, but the social infrastructure surrounding many industrial communities has not developed at the same pace.
We need to consider whether the well-being of workers and their children should be part of how we think about industrial development, rather than a separate social issue outside the factory gate.
My experience working with communities around industrial areas has increasingly convinced me that it should.
In the densely populated worker settlements of Mirpur in Dhaka and Kashimpur in Gazipur, an initiative supported by the Garcia Foundation, associated with Dutch enterprise JOG Group BV, brought Terre des Hommes Netherlands and Breaking the Silence, a Bangladesh based non-government organization, together to strengthen child protection at community level. The initiative responded to concerns about the care, early learning, and protection available to young children while their parents worked long hours in garment factories.
Community-based early childhood development (ECD) centres were one part of the response which provided children aged four to six with four hours of early learning, care, and basic safety awareness. They also helped prepare children for the transition to formal primary education. These were not full-day daycare facilities, and they did not cover the entire period when parents were at work. Their significance lay in the role they played within a wider effort to strengthen child protection in the surrounding communities.
The centres provided a trusted point of contact through which families could engage with broader community-based child protection activities. By connecting families, community structures, and wider child protection services, the initiative sought to build a system that could help communities recognize risks, respond to them, and create safer environments for children.
This experience raises a broader question: Could similar approaches work in other industrial communities in Bangladesh? Children are part of the industrial ecosystem even when they are outside the factory. Their well-being matters to families and communities, while parents may find it harder to concentrate on their work. Addressing these concerns requires us to look beyond the factory floor and consider the conditions in which workers’ families live.
An ECD centre cannot address every need, and a four-hour program cannot cover a parent's entire working day. Children may still face barriers to education, health, and social services, as well as risks of neglect or exploitation. The challenge is not simply a lack of services, but also the gaps between the people and institutions responsible for supporting children.
We are exploring this approach in another industrial setting through an emerging opportunity involving another Dutch enterprise, Royal LC Packaging, and their partner, Dutch Bangla Pack in Gazaria, Munshiganj. The intention is not simply to establish an ECD facility, but to explore a broader community-based child protection approach informed by the experience of the Garcia Foundation-supported initiative in Mirpur and Kashimpur.
Depending on local needs, this could involve engaging parents, strengthening community protection mechanisms, creating opportunities for children and young people to participate, and connecting families with relevant services.
The approach should not be replicated unchanged. Industrial communities differ in their needs, existing services, and relationships with employers and government. Any response must reflect these local realities while bringing families, communities, employers, civil society organizations, and public services together around children's needs.
This experience also raises questions about how companies and philanthropic organizations invest in communities. Rather than starting with a particular project, they could begin by asking what prevents children and families from getting the support they need.
In one community, the priority may be early childhood services; in another, it may be stronger protection mechanisms, support for parents, or better access to government services.
Corporate and philanthropic funding can help bring actors together, test approaches, and generate evidence. But these efforts should not create parallel systems that depend indefinitely on a single donor or company.
Employers can contribute resources and support workers and their families. Civil society organizations can provide expertise and maintain community relationships. Parents, young people, and local leaders can help identify risks and shape responses.
The government retains responsibility for protecting children's rights and providing public services. These roles should complement one another, with the aim of building arrangements that can continue beyond an individual project's funding period.
Bangladesh could test this approach in a small number of industrial communities where all concerned parties are willing to work together. The results should be assessed not only by the services established, but also by whether children are safer, families can access support, and community protection mechanisms are stronger. This should include examining what children need beyond ECD centre hours, so that future investment responds to the realities of workers' families.
Bangladesh’s industrial growth has created enormous economic opportunities, but the communities that sustain this growth need better support. They are places where children grow up, families make decisions, and the next generation is shaped. If we want these communities to be productive, resilient, and inclusive, we need to pay greater attention to the social infrastructure around them.
The opportunity is to build stronger connections between children, families, communities, employers, and public services so that the benefits of industrial growth extend beyond production and into people’s lives.
The factory gate should not be the boundary of our thinking about workers, their families, and their children. It should be the starting point.
Nazrul Islam is the Country Manager for Bangladesh and Partnership Specialist for Bangladesh and Thailand at Terre des Hommes Netherlands. Email: n.islam@tdh.nl .

item.title: Washington's political reset & South Asia. [ today ]
Political theatrics, asylum claims and the cost to British Bangladeshis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The violent street fighting between Awami League and National Citizen Party (NCP) activists in Romford, east London, on November 16 has exposed an uncomfortable reality: political rivalries imported from Bangladesh are damaging the reputation of the wider British Bangladeshi community.
The confrontation erupted on a road behind Mayfair Hall following a reception for NCP Convener and Opposition Chief Whip Nahid Islam MP.
The fighting reportedly continued for around 20 minutes, leaving several people injured and requiring police intervention.
According to eyewitness accounts, local Awami League activists initiated the confrontation, catching NCP supporters off guard.
Protesters allegedly threw eggs and water bottles at arriving guests and assaulted attendees outside the venue.
Nahid himself avoided direct confrontation, having entered the hall several hours before the program and departed through a rear exit.
British emergency services confirmed responding to the disorder.
The London Ambulance Service treated six people at the scene, while police reported that three were taken to hospital.
Yet the consequences of this confrontation extend far beyond those directly involved.
For British Bangladeshis who have spent generations building their lives in the United Kingdom, such incidents turn community spaces into battlegrounds for political rivalries originating thousands of miles away.
Community observers have described the Romford confrontation as an example of staged political provocation rather than genuine democratic engagement.
The concern is that some activists may deliberately create confrontations to attract publicity, demonstrate loyalty to political leaders or strengthen their political standing.
More controversially, allegations have circulated that certain individuals participate in such clashes to generate police reports, medical records and photographs that could support applications for political asylum in Britain.
These allegations require independent investigation.
There is no verified evidence that the Romford confrontation was organised for asylum purposes, and genuine asylum claims must not be confused with allegations of deliberate political manipulation.
Nevertheless, the question deserves scrutiny.
If political violence is being manufactured for personal advantage, it undermines both legitimate democratic activism and public confidence in the asylum system.
Political loyalty, personal ambition or immigration considerations cannot justify turning British streets into arenas of intimidation and violence.
The immediate consequence of the Romford disorder was its exploitation by British anti-immigration voices.
Political figures associated with Reform UK used the confrontation to criticise immigration policies and portray the violence as an example of foreign political disputes being imported into Britain.
Such reactions demonstrate how quickly the conduct of a small group can become a damaging narrative about an entire community.
When videos of Bangladeshi men fighting circulate across social media without context, the consequences are not confined to the participants.
Families, shopkeepers, students and professionals in London, Luton, Birmingham and Oldham may find themselves facing suspicion because of political conflicts they neither support nor participate in.
For generations, British Bangladeshis have worked to establish themselves within British society.
Their contributions to business, education, culture and public life should not be overshadowed by the actions of political activists seeking attention or confrontation.
Yet every incident of this kind risks reinforcing damaging stereotypes and weakening the community’s standing.
The reputational cost is collective, even when responsibility for the violence is individual.
The deeper tragedy is how much energy some sections of the British Bangladeshi community continue to devote to Bangladesh’s domestic political rivalries instead of constructive engagement with British public life.
Anyone who makes Britain their home has opportunities to participate in mainstream politics, influence local councils, shape public policy and contribute to national democratic institutions.
Communities of Indian and Pakistani heritage have established substantial political influence in Britain, including representation in Parliament, ministerial positions and important policymaking roles.
British Bangladeshis have also achieved political representation and made significant contributions.
Nevertheless, there remains considerable scope to strengthen their influence across politics, business and wider public life.
That progress requires sustained civic participation, not street confrontations over political disputes in Dhaka.
While others are building influence within Westminster and local government, why should sections of the British Bangladeshi community remain preoccupied with factional battles that offer little benefit to their families or future generations?
Political differences are natural, and expatriates have every right to remain engaged with Bangladesh’s affairs.
But there is a fundamental difference between peaceful political participation and importing hostility into the streets of another country.
The former strengthens democracy. The latter damages public trust.
The Romford incident has drawn strong criticism from British Bangladeshi residents and community figures.
British Bangladeshi resident Farzana Boby Amie described the violence as disgusting and deeply shameful, stressing that political differences could never justify aggression, intimidation or physical confrontation.
Cultural organiser Mahbubur Rahman Shiblu similarly expressed concern that bringing Bangladesh’s political hostility into Britain was damaging the country’s reputation and leaving ordinary British Bangladeshis to bear the consequences.
Their frustration reflects a wider concern that community events are increasingly becoming opportunities for confrontation rather than dialogue.
The incident also disrupted Nahid Islam’s week-long visit to the United Kingdom, which began on November 13 and was scheduled to conclude on November 21.
Following the confrontation, his planned appearance on a local Bengali television channel was reportedly cancelled after Awami League activists gathered outside the station.
He also visited injured attendees at King’s College Hospital.
Such disruptions illustrate how political hostility can extend beyond individual events, affecting community engagement and the freedom to participate in political discussions.
British Bangladeshis have established roots in the United Kingdom over more than a century, with many families now in their fourth generation.
Yet questions remain about whether the community has fully realised its potential in mainstream politics, the economy and public life compared with other established South Asian communities.
These questions deserve serious reflection, not another round of political blame.
The younger generation needs successful role models, greater opportunities and a community whose public identity is defined by achievement rather than confrontation.
Instead, repeated political clashes risk leaving children and young people to inherit reputational damage created by disputes in which they had no involvement.
Why should an entire community suffer humiliation because some individuals cannot separate political allegiance from public responsibility?
Those determined to pursue Bangladesh’s party politics should do so through legitimate democratic channels, rather than turning British neighbourhoods into battlegrounds.
Nor should political confrontations become instruments for personal publicity, questionable asylum-related ambitions or hopes of securing a party leader’s favour and a future parliamentary nomination.
Such motives must be established through evidence before being attributed to individuals. But the wider principle is beyond dispute: political ambitions cannot justify violence or the collective embarrassment of a community.
British Bangladeshis should not have to defend their reputation every time rival political activists exchange blows on a London street.
The community has invested generations in building its future in Britain. That future must not be sacrificed for political theatrics rooted in conflicts thousands of miles away.
Enough humiliation has already been inflicted in the name of politics. There is no reason to pass more of it on to the next generation.

Shane Deitz appointed Pakistan women’s team head coach. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) on Tuesday appointed Australian Shane Deitz as head coach of the national women’s cricket team, with the 51-year-old set to take charge ahead of the forthcoming bilateral series against West Indies.

Deitz will join the Pakistan squad in the Caribbean for his first assignment, replacing Wahab Riaz, who had been serving as mentor and head coach following the departure of former Test batter Mohammad Wasim after last year’s ICC Women’s World Cup.

He becomes the third foreign coach to take charge of the Pakistan women’s team, following New Zealand’s Mark Coles, who had two stints in the role, and Bermuda’s David Hemp. His appointment also marks a return to a foreign coaching option after a period of local coaches.

In a statement issued by the PCB, Deitz said he was honoured to take up the position, recalling his memories of supporting Pakistan during the 1992 World Cup final against England.

“I am very honoured to become the head coach of the Pakistan women’s team. Pakistan cricket has a tremendous history and I remember fondly cheering them on as a youngster in Australia at the 1992 World Cup final against England, which was a great achievement for Pakistan cricket,” he said.

Deitz said the team’s long-term objective would be to give supporters something to cheer about when Pakistan hosts the T20 World Cup in 2028. He acknowledged that considerable work lay ahead for the players and coaching staff to produce world-class performances.

Playing and coaching background

Hailing from Bankstown, New South Wales, Deitz was a left-handed top-order batter who also occasionally kept wickets.

After representing New South Wales at junior level, he moved to South Australia, where he played 66 first-class matches for the Redbacks between 1998-99 and 2007-08.

Following his retirement, Deitz moved into coaching, initially serving as a high-performance coach with Cricket Wellington in New Zealand from 2008 to 2013.

He subsequently coached Bangladesh’s women’s team in 2013-14 before taking up various roles with Vanuatu Cricket, including national coach and chief executive.

From around 2020 to 2023, he coached the Netherlands women’s team, helping the side regain ODI status.

In July 2023, Deitz was appointed head coach of the West Indies women’s team. Under his guidance, the Caribbean side reached the semi-finals of consecutive ICC Women’s T20 World Cups in 2024 and 2026.

His contract with Cricket West Indies expired at the end of October 2026, with both parties mutually agreeing to part ways.

Frequent changes in coaching set-up

The Pakistan women’s team has witnessed considerable instability in its coaching set-up in recent years, with Deitz becoming the sixth person to take charge in the past three and a half years.

Coles, the first foreign coach of the team, served from 2017 to 2019 before briefly returning in 2023. However, he resigned during his second stint for personal reasons.

Hemp succeeded Coles and remained in the role from 2020 until around 2022.

Subsequent appointments included local coaches and interim arrangements, with Wasim taking charge ahead of the 2024 Asia Cup before his departure following the World Cup.

Wahab subsequently oversaw the team as mentor and head coach during a mixed period that included a solitary victory at the T20 World Cup, a semi-final appearance at the Asia Cup and a bronze medal at the Asian Games, alongside a number of series defeats.

Pakistan are currently featuring in the ICC Emerging Nations Trophy in the United Arab Emirates.

item.title: Are we preparing our next generation to compete?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is approaching a defining moment in its development journey. We have a large working-age population, an expanding university system and a generation of young people who aspire to become professionals, entrepreneurs, researchers and public servants. Yet an uncomfortable question remains: Are we actually preparing this generation to compete in a rapidly changing world, or are we simply producing more graduates for an increasingly crowded job market?
United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) estimates that Bangladesh had a population of 175.7 million in 2025, with approximately 66% aged 15–64. This represents an enormous potential workforce. But potential is not performance. If young people cannot access quality education, appropriate skills and decent employment, the demographic dividend can become a demographic burden. The World Bank has already warned that Bangladesh has not fully translated its favourable age structure into employment and productivity.
According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics' Labour Force Survey 2024, the national unemployment rate was 3.66%. However, unemployment among young people aged 15–24 was 9.65%, while the rate among university graduates reached approximately 13.54%. Nearly 8.85 lakh graduates were unemployed in 2024, according to reported BBS figures. Even more concerning is the number of young people who are neither studying, employed nor receiving training. The Labour Force Survey 2024 indicates that nearly 86 lakh young people fall into this category, approximately one in five young people. This is not simply an unemployment problem. It is a problem of lost opportunity, wasted potential and inadequate pathways from education to employment.
What does this tell us? Our education system and labour market are not communicating effectively. Universities produce graduates, but employers often seek competencies that graduates have not acquired. Young people pursue degrees, but many are unable to translate those qualifications into suitable employment. Employers report difficulty finding appropriately skilled candidates, while graduates struggle to find jobs matching their education.
Bangladesh has expanded its higher education sector considerably. More universities, more students and greater access to tertiary education should be recognised as important achievements. However, expansion in the number of institutions is not the same as improvement in academic excellence.
According to reporting on the QS World University Rankings 2026, 15 Bangladeshi universities appeared in the global rankings, with the University of Dhaka ranked 584th. In the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2026, no Bangladeshi university appeared among the world's top 800. These rankings should not be treated as complete measures of academic quality, but they do raise questions about research output, citation impact, international collaboration, academic reputation and institutional competitiveness.
Yet research requires investment, research-oriented leadership, qualified academics, well-equipped laboratories, access to scholarly databases, international collaboration and an institutional culture that values critical inquiry. Without these foundations, universities struggle to compete internationally. The issue is not simply the number of research publications. We must also examine their quality, relevance, originality and influence. Are our universities producing research that informs public policy? Are they developing technologies that industries can use? Are academics collaborating with international research networks? Are postgraduate students receiving appropriate research supervision? Are universities creating knowledge that addresses Bangladesh's development challenges?
The world of work is changing rapidly. Artificial intelligence, automation, digital platforms, renewable energy, advanced manufacturing, data science and climate-related industries are transforming the skills required in almost every sector. We should rethink the meaning of competence. A competent graduate should be able to analyse information, communicate effectively, use technology, work collaboratively, exercise ethical judgement and apply knowledge to practical problems. These capabilities are relevant to government, business, academia, civil society and entrepreneurship.
A systematic and coordinated way forward is essential to ensure that our demographic dividend is translated into a skilled, productive and globally competitive workforce. First, reform education around competencies rather than certificates. Curriculum reform should prioritise critical thinking, communication, analytical reasoning, digital literacy, creativity, problem-solving and ethical leadership. Universities must regularly review programs in consultation with employers, professional bodies, alumni and researchers.
Second, establish a stronger education-to-employment transition system. Every university should have a functional career development and placement centre. Students should receive career counselling, internship opportunities, professional mentoring and information about public, private and international career pathways. Graduate tracer studies should identify employment outcomes and skills gaps.
Third, strengthen technical and vocational education. Not every young person needs a conventional university degree. Bangladesh should develop high-quality technical and professional pathways in advanced manufacturing, construction, healthcare, agriculture, logistics, renewable energy, information technology and other expanding sectors. Vocational education must be treated as a respected career pathway, not a second-choice option.
Fourth, reform public-sector recruitment and professional development. Recruitment should be transparent, timely and competency-based. Public institutions need specialist professionals as well as general administrators. Continuous professional development should ensure that public servants acquire skills in digital government, policy analysis, project management, public financial management, data analytics and service innovation.
Fifth, make universities research-driven and internationally connected. Research funding should be increased and distributed transparently through competitive grants and peer review. Universities should establish research centres, strengthen postgraduate supervision, support early-career researchers and develop international research partnerships. Academic performance should be assessed through teaching quality, research contribution, innovation and public engagement not merely administrative seniority.
Sixth, create more productive employment opportunities. Skill development alone cannot solve unemployment if the economy does not create sufficient jobs. Bangladesh needs a stronger investment environment, growing industries, support for small and medium enterprises, entrepreneurship finance and opportunities in high-value sectors. Private-sector employment should become an attractive and respected career option. Women also need safer workplaces, affordable childcare, flexible employment arrangements and equal opportunities for advancement.
Seventh, establish a national human-capital accountability framework. The government should monitor graduate employment, youth unemployment, NEET rates, skills shortages, research expenditure, international student enrolment, graduate earnings and public-sector vacancy-filling. These indicators should be published regularly and used to evaluate education, employment and skill policies. Without reliable data, reform will remain dependent on assumptions rather than evidence.
The most important question for Bangladesh is therefore not how many graduates we produce every year, but how many competent, confident and innovative citizens we prepare to lead the country forward.
Fataraz Zahan is assistant professor, Bangladesh Institute of Governance and Management (BIGM).

item.title: Welcome to Dhaka: The real promise of HSIA’s Terminal 3. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Earlier this year, I wrote about Bangladesh’s tourism potential in a local daily and later shared the article on LinkedIn. The post generated an interesting discussion, but one comment left a lasting impression. A senior professor and business leader from Malaysia recalled his experience at Dhaka airport immigration. What he encountered, he said, was an atmosphere of rudeness and indifference. His conclusion was blunt: “Never went again.”
However, this misses the real issue. The problem lies not with the warm hospitality of individual Bangladeshis, but with the poor arrival experience at the country's main port of entry. A potential investor walked through the nation’s front door and left deeply alienated, a failed first impression that costs the country future goodwill and capital.
A world-class terminal, what next?
That is why the long-awaited opening of Terminal 3 at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (HSIA) matters for more than aviation. After a prolonged deadlock over service charges and revenue-sharing, the operating agreement with the Japanese consortium is now expected to be signed in November 2026 , pending final government approvals. Its draft terms have already drawn debate, including a reported 15-year restriction on competing commercial airports within 100km of Dhaka and calls for fuller public disclosure. The terminal is set to open in phases, beginning with a limited number of international flights on 16 December 2026 and expanding as operations settle, with fuller service likely in early 2027.
The project itself is enormous. Built at a cost of $2.3 billion , the third terminal spans nearly 542,000 square meters and is designed to add capacity for 12 to 16 million passengers a year. Yet, despite being over 99% complete, it has remained idle for nearly a year and a half, long enough for warranties on advanced installed systems to begin expiring.
After years of waiting, Bangladesh is therefore close to getting a new gateway capable of transforming the country's aviation infrastructure. But amid the debate over the deal’s cost and terms, a different question deserves more attention: What will it feel like to arrive in Bangladesh?
The first hour matters
The concern is not theoretical. In April 2024, ten tourists from Taiwan arrived to celebrate Pohela Boishakh, the Bengali new year, and spent around two hours at the visa-on-arrival desk. Six counters were available, but only three officers were working. There was reportedly nowhere to sit and no drinking water.
There were other complaints about long queues and difficulties at immigration as captured in Skytrax reviews . The issue is not that every traveler has the same experience. Nor is it fair to generalize about airport staff, many of whom work under considerable pressure. The bigger problem is that the system often appears to be designed around the process rather than the passenger.
Bangladesh receives only about 630,000 international arrivals a year, a fraction of the numbers attracted by regional peers like Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam. The gap cannot be explained simply by a lack of attractions. For many visitors, their impression of Bangladesh begins at the airport, and that first impression can shape everything that follows. A traveler does not care which agency is responsible for a delay. They do not distinguish between immigration, airport management, ground handling or another government department. They see one thing: Bangladesh.
Online reviews tell a similar story, with complaints about queues, baggage delays, facilities and staff interactions. In the digital age, a bad airport experience does not end at the airport. It travels through social media and travel forums, shaping perceptions before the next visitor ever boards a plane.
Capacity isn’t capability
Some of the frustration might be the result of overcrowding. HSIA was designed to handle around 8 million passengers a year. In 2025, it moved 12.72 million . With only eight baggage belts , 13 to 15 international flights landing around the same time on a foggy winter morning can turn the arrival hall into gridlock.
Terminal 3 should relieve much of that pressure. Once fully operational, the airport's overall passenger capacity is expected to rise to more than 20 million a year. But infrastructure alone does not create a good airport. A larger terminal can create larger queues if the processes inside it remain inefficient. More immigration counters do not necessarily mean faster immigration if staffing does not match demand. New baggage systems do not help much if the surrounding processes remain poorly coordinated. In other words, capacity and capability are not the same thing. Terminal 3 gives Bangladesh a rare opportunity to address both.
The overlooked passengers
There is another group whose experience deserves specific attention: Bangladeshis returning from overseas employment. Around 1.13 million Bangladeshis went for jobs abroad in 2025 alone. More than 15 million Bangladeshis now work overseas, and in the 2025-26 fiscal year they sent home a record US$35.56 billion , the country’s largest source of foreign earnings.
Returning workers have described luggage that arrives opened and lighter, two-to-three-hour waits at the baggage belt, and, as one Saudi returnee told a public hearing , officials who fail to show ‘the bare minimum respect.’ Dedicated lounges and volunteer help have since appeared, though mostly on the departure side.
These are not abstract numbers. Behind them are people who leave their families, work long hours in foreign countries and return home carrying savings, gifts and years of accumulated memories. For them, the arrival hall should feel like homecoming, not another hurdle. If Terminal 3 is meant to represent a more confident Bangladesh, that welcome should begin with them.
Technology shortens queues, people shape experiences
Singapore’s Changi Airport has brought average immigration clearance time down to around ten seconds and now aims for 95% of passengers to use automated lanes. South Korea’s Incheon Airport combines similar automation with a strong focus on passenger service.
The lesson for Bangladesh is not to copy either airport, but to recognize that technology works best when it is designed around the passenger. Biometric immigration, automated gates and pre-arrival processing can reduce unnecessary queues while allowing officers to focus on passengers who genuinely require closer attention.
Terminal 3 should adopt these systems from the beginning rather than treating them as an afterthought. But technology alone cannot create a welcoming airport. A fast e-gate means little if a confused traveler cannot find the right direction. A modern immigration hall means little if an officer treats a passenger’s question as an inconvenience.
The real shift must be cultural: the passenger should not have to adapt to the bureaucracy. The system should be designed around the passenger.
Measuring the welcome
There are also simple reforms that cost far less than a new terminal. From day one, Terminal 3 should measure and publish basic service indicators: Immigration waiting times, baggage delivery times, passenger satisfaction and complaint resolution.
Competition can help too. The move to add a second passenger ground-handling operator alongside Biman, ending its long-standing monopoly, is a positive step. The Japanese consortium has shortlisted four global firms for the role: Menzies Aviation, Swissport, Çelebi Aviation Holding and dnata. But competition must be accompanied by common service standards across immigration, security, ground handling and passenger assistance. Courtesy should not depend on which agency happens to be behind the counter.
The real promise
Bangladesh has demonstrated that it can build major infrastructure. The harder challenge is making the establishments inside those buildings work differently. Terminal 3 should therefore be judged by more than passenger numbers and aircraft movements.
Will a tourist leave thinking, I want to come back?
Will a business traveler leave with greater confidence in Bangladesh?
Will a migrant worker returning after years abroad feel that his country has remembered him?
These may not appear on a balance sheet, but they have real economic value. Bangladesh has spent billions creating a new front door. The greater challenge now is to decide what kind of welcome awaits behind it. Because when people leave Terminal 3, they may not remember the glass, steel or technology. They will remember how the country made them feel.
Dr Sabbir Ahmad, a tech executive with global experience in digital connectivity, sustainable infrastructure and energy, now shaping Bangladesh's semiconductor landscape as the CEO of Silicon Array Ltd.
